Trimmed from the run log, not edited. TLSNotary v0.1.0-alpha.15, MPC-TLS, TLS 1.2.

### Two-agent payment demo

1 paid · 4 refused

Agent A quotes the USD→EUR rate from api.frankfurter.dev (ECB reference rates). Agent B pays a €10,000 invoice in dollars at that rate. Every message between them passes through a relay that tries to cheat. Agent B acts only on a value inside a valid receipt, from the right server, for the right request, less than ten minutes old.

Round  | The relay  | Agent B
--- | --- | ---
1  | Forwards the message unchanged  | Computes the payment at the witnessed rate
2  | Changes the rate, leaves the receipt  | Refuses: the claim does not match the receipt
3  | Changes the rate and edits the receipt to match  | Refuses: the receipt fails verification
4  | Swaps in a genuine receipt for USD→GBP  | Refuses: the receipt answers a different request
5  | Strips the receipt  | Refuses: unwitnessed claim

The agents are scripted MCP clients, not language models, so runs repeat exactly. No money moved; agent B computes the payment.

Measured on one machine with the witness running locally. A remote witness has not been measured yet.

Limits

## What a receipt does not prove.

A receipt proves what a named server sent, and when. Read it as exactly that.

It does not prove

  * That the server told the truth. A receipt shows what api.weather.gov said, not the weather.
  * Anything about a server the operator controls. That receipt is still the operator’s word, now fixed in time and bytes.
  * That the agent sent every action through the witness. That takes credential custody or egress control.
  * Independence, when one party runs both the agent side and the witness. High-value receipts should carry more than one witness.
  * That the content is safe to act on. A genuine page can still carry a prompt injection.

Engine limits today: TLS 1.2 only (TLS 1.3 is on TLSNotary’s roadmap), pre-release software, and no compressed or streamed responses.

## Two tools your agent already knows how to call.

Histor ships as a CLI and an MCP server, so it works in Claude Code, Cursor and any MCP client. Receipts are content-addressed: agents pass a short receipt_id instead of 15 KB of base64.

witnessed_fetch(url, fields?, mode?)

GETs an https:// URL through a Histor witness. Returns the server, time, request and disclosed fields, plus a receipt_id.

verify_receipt(receipt_id | receipt, expect_server?)

Checks a receipt another agent handed you, offline. Returns what it proves, or the reason it fails.

witnessed_request(url, method, body, request_fields?)

POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE. Credentials for the target live on the server, so the model never sees a secret. The request body is committed and stays hidden unless you disclose named fields.

## Underwrite from evidence the insured didn’t write.

New AI-liability covers ask for agent logs, and today those logs are self-reported. Cyber insurers learned to price from external scans the insured couldn’t edit. A Histor receipt gives an AI-liability book the same kind of signal for agent actions.

### At claim time

Check what the agent was told before it acted. The claims desk verifies the receipt itself, offline.

### At underwriting

Witnessed actions as a share of all agent actions is a number the insured can’t inflate.

### Narrow by design

A receipt proves what a named server sent and when. It makes no claim about whether the agent acted well.

An agent can say it swapped your tokens or fixed your bug. Karatum checks the system of record — the blockchain, the test suite — not the agent's word. Every verdict is decided by a validator independent of the agent, attested on-chain (Ethereum Sepolia testnet today), and turned into a reliability rating in karats.

01 Graded agents

## Self-reports are wrong in both directions.

Claude Code (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) and four reference agents ran the same Adversarial & Volatile series: 10 trials on a Base mainnet fork with price moves mid-swap, injected prompts and traps that must be refused. The validator read chain state; the agent's own report was recorded and ignored.

02 The missing layer

## The rails exist. The outcome layer doesn't.

Identity says who an agent is. Receipts say what it ran. Nothing in the stack says whether the work actually landed — and who deserves the next job.

Identity Who is the agent?ERC-8004 · Moca AIR

Communication How does it talk to tools and agents?MCP · A2A

Payments How does value move?x402 · USDC

Commerce How are jobs escrowed and settled?ERC-8183 · Virtuals ACP

Outcome Did it actually work? Who gets the next job?KARATUM

Neutral across chains, models and agent ecosystems. Karatum plugs into every rail and replaces none of them.

03 How it works

## From a task to a payout, every step checkable.

A tool call that returned 200 is not a refund that landed. Each stage below produces something a contract, a buyer or another agent can verify.

05 K-rating

## Reliability, graded like gold.

24 karats is pure. A K-rating is the lower bound of the 95% Wilson interval of verified success, scaled to 24 — per build, per task class.

  * 01 Small samples score low on purpose. Three lucky runs cannot earn a high grade.
  * 02 Only verified outcomes count. Claims, retries and revoked verdicts never move the number.
  * 03 Certificates expire and go stale. A silent model or prompt swap shows up as behavioural drift.

# Privacy policy — Karatum mobile app

Karatum is an Outcome Oracle for AI agents. The mobile app shows verified track records of agents, verifies transactions, and lets you try pay-on-outcome jobs with test tokens on the Ethereum Sepolia testnet. It has no user accounts, no advertising, no analytics and no tracking.

## What stays on your device

  * Preferences: the API address you chose, your alert preference, the builds you watch, your recent verifications and the test jobs you funded (public data only: addresses, amounts, transaction hashes, job ids). Stored in the app's local storage.
  * Your API key, if you add one: stored only in the device keychain / keystore.
  * The test wallet key, if you create a test wallet: generated on the device and stored only in the device keychain / keystore, excluded from backups. It is never shown, never exported and never sent to Karatum or anyone else. It works on the Sepolia testnet only.

Deleting the app, or using the in-app controls (remove key, clear history, delete test wallet), erases this data. We cannot recover it for you.

## What the app sends over the network

  * Karatum API (karatum.com, or the address you set): requests to read agents, ratings, certificates and verdicts; the transaction hashes you ask it to verify; and, when you hire an agent, the job terms (amounts, the agent's and your test wallet's public addresses, deadline and task). If you added an API key, it is sent with requests that need it.
  * A public Sepolia RPC node (ethereum-sepolia-rpc.publicnode.com): balance and contract reads for public addresses, and the testnet transactions your test wallet signs. Transactions on a blockchain are public and permanent.
  * Links you open (Sepolia Etherscan, testnet faucets, attestation pages) open in the in-app browser under those sites' own policies.

Like any web service, these servers receive your IP address with each request. The Karatum API uses it only for security and rate limiting; it does not build profiles and does not sell or share data.

# Karatum, in one place.

Logos, colors, approved copy, key facts and product screenshots. Use the assets as provided: keep the hallmark's proportions and clear space, and write the name as Karatum (one word, capital K).

## One-liner and boilerplate

One-liner

Karatum is the Outcome Oracle for AI agents: it proves what an agent actually achieved, not what it says it did.

Short boilerplate (about 55 words)

Karatum independently verifies the work of AI agents. A validator independent of the agent checks the system of record — blockchain state, test suites — never the agent's own claim, attests verdicts on-chain (Ethereum Sepolia testnet today) and grades reliability in karats. Buyers, marketplaces and other agents use Karatum to choose who to hire and to pay only for verified outcomes.

Long boilerplate

# KaratumBot

KaratumBot is the crawler behind Karatum's Unsolicited Ratings. It visits the endpoints that an AI agent's own on-chain ERC-8004 registration file declares, checks whether they answer and follow the protocol they claim, and publishes the result. If you are reading this because it appeared in your logs: your host, or an agent that points at it, is in the public ERC-8004 registry.

## How to recognise it

User-Agent, on every request:
    
    KaratumBot/1.0 (+https://karatum.com/bot; unsolicited agent ratings; read-only; contact via that page)

It runs from one server, outbound address 152.53.39.171 (IPv6 2a0a:4cc0:2000:d94:3471:ebff:fe20:f3b5). robots.txt product token: KaratumBot.

## What it does

### Requests

  * GET /robots.txt once a day per site, and we obey it.
  * GET of the URLs your registration file lists: an A2A agent card, an MCP server, an OpenAPI document, an x402 resource. Web pages, repositories and marketplace listings that a registration file links are not requested.
